title: Gates, Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps
subtitle: Six gates, a handful of algebra rules and one picture (the K-map) — enough to design and shrink any combinational circuit.

gates.title: The basic gates
gates.body: AND outputs 1 only if all inputs are 1; OR if any is 1; NOT inverts; NAND and NOR are the inverted AND/OR; XOR is 1 when the inputs differ. NAND and NOR are universal: any circuit can be built from one of them alone. Try the AND gate: only A = B = 1 lights the output.

nand.title: Universality of NAND
nand.body: NAND with its inputs tied together is NOT. NAND followed by a NOT-made-of-NAND is AND. By De Morgan, NAND with inverted inputs is OR. Hence chip makers stock one kind of gate and wire it up to do everything.

alg.title: Boolean algebra
alg.body:
LawForm
IdentityA + 0 = A, A·1 = A
NullA + 1 = 1, A·0 = 0
ComplementA + A′ = 1, A·A′ = 0
AbsorptionA + AB = A
De Morgan(AB)′ = A′ + B′, (A + B)′ = A′B′
alg.steps: Simplify F = AB + AB′. Factor A: A(B + B′). B + B′ = 1, so F = A.

sop.title: Sum of products and minterms
sop.body: Every truth table is an OR of minterms (AND terms for each row where F = 1). This sum of products (SOP) is correct but usually bigger than needed. Shorthand F = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7) lists the rows. Dually, the product of maxterms (POS) uses rows where F = 0.
sop.steps: F = 1 at minterms 1, 3, 5, 7 of three variables (A, B, C). Those are the rows with C = 1, so F = C.

kmap.title: Karnaugh maps
kmap.body: A K-map lays the truth table out so that neighbouring cells differ in one variable (Gray-code order, wrapping around the edges). Circle rectangular groups of 1s of size 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 — the larger, the simpler — and each group gives one product term with only the variables that stay constant. For the minterms 1, 3, 5, 7 the four cells form one group: F = C. The default 4-variable example minimises to B'C' + CD' + A'BD (3 terms).
kmap.steps: Four adjacent 1s in a row or square share two constant variables, so a group of 4 removes two variables. A group of 2ᵏ cells eliminates k variables.

dc.title: Don’t-cares
dc.body: Some input combinations never occur (a BCD digit never exceeds 9). Mark them X: you may treat each X as 1 if it lets a group grow, or 0 if not. This often yields a much simpler circuit. Only include an X in a group when it helps.
